title: Choose synchronous processing vs a message queue
description: Decide between immediate synchronous processing and asynchronous message-queue patterns for order fulfillment, considering latency, reliability, and user experience.

data.text: Your checkout flow currently processes payment, inventory reservation, and shipping label generation synchronously in a single API call. Under Black Friday traffic, a shipping API timeout causes the entire checkout to fail. Customers abandon their carts. You need to decide whether to add retries and circuit breakers to the sync path, or move fulfillment to a message queue.

terms.definition: An intermediary that buffers messages between producers and consumers for asynchronous processing.
A queue for messages that could not be processed after multiple retries.
A consistency model where updates propagate asynchronously; all replicas converge eventually.
A pattern that stops sending requests to a failing service after a threshold, preventing cascading failure.
A sequence of local transactions with compensating actions to maintain consistency without distributed transactions.

data.title: The timeout trap
data.text: Extending timeouts on synchronous calls does not fix the underlying problem. It only makes failures slower to detect and increases the chance of thread pool exhaustion and cascading retries.

cards.title: Synchronous with Resilience
cards.description: Keep the current flow but add timeouts, retries, and circuit breakers.
pros: User gets immediate confirmation that checkout succeeded
Simpler code path; no eventual consistency concerns
Easier to debug with standard request tracing
cons: Slowest dependency blocks the entire flow
Retries amplify load on already-struggling services
User experience degrades under any downstream issue
Thread and connection pools fill during spikes

cards.title: Message Queue (Async)
cards.description: Decouple checkout from fulfillment using a broker like RabbitMQ or SQS.
pros: Checkout returns immediately; user sees success page
Broker absorbs traffic spikes with durable buffering
Failed jobs land in dead-letter queues for manual inspection
Shipping service can be scaled independently
cons: Users must poll or receive webhooks for order status
Requires idempotency to handle duplicate deliveries
Operational complexity: brokers, consumers, and DLQs
End-to-end tracing spans synchronous and async boundaries

data.title: C#: Resilient synchronous call with Polly
data.content: Circuit breaker and timeout protect the checkout API from shipping failures.

data.title: RabbitMQ: Order events published after payment
data.content: Payment succeeds synchronously; fulfillment is asynchronous.
data.code:
# Exchange: orders
# Routing keys: order.created, order.paid, order.shipped

Producer (Checkout API):
1. Process payment synchronously
2. Publish OrderPaid event to RabbitMQ
3. Return 200 to client immediately

Consumer (Fulfillment Worker):
1. Consume OrderPaid
2. Reserve inventory
3. Generate shipping label
4. Publish OrderShipped event
5. If step 2 fails -> DLQ after 3 retries

data.caption: Synchronous chain failure versus asynchronous buffering
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[User Checkout] --> B[Payment]
    B --> C[Inventory]
    C --> D[Shipping]
    D --> E{Success?}
    E -->|No| F[User sees error]

    G[User Checkout] --> H[Payment]
    H --> I[Return 200]
    I --> J[Message Queue]
    J --> K[Inventory Worker]
    K --> L[Shipping Worker]
    L --> M{Success?}
    M -->|No| N[Dead-Letter Queue]

items.text: Can users tolerate eventual confirmation of order success?
Are downstream services experiencing cascading timeouts?
Do you have idempotency guarantees on all consumer operations?
Is your team comfortable operating a message broker?
What is the business cost of a failed checkout versus a delayed shipment?

data.title: Recommended approach: Async for fulfillment, sync for payment
data.content: Payment must remain synchronous: the user needs immediate confirmation of charge. Everything after payment—inventory, notifications, shipping—should be asynchronous. This limits the synchronous failure domain to the most critical operation and gives fulfillment workers a durable buffer.

data.title: Idempotency is non-negotiable
data.text: Message brokers guarantee at-least-once delivery. Every consumer must be idempotent: processing the same message twice must produce the same result as processing it once.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: Synchronous paths should be as short as possible.
Use async queues to buffer non-critical downstream work.
Dead-letter queues are your safety net; monitor them.
data.takeaway: Accept the payment synchronously. Fulfill everything else asynchronously.
